rows.theme_label: The pubs, its convenient and simpler
rows.theme_description: It is common as it is easy to decide to go there and you can drink, get food, chat and sometimes watch sports
rows.supporting_quote: Yeah, so for me it's usually the pub, to be honest. There's a few we rotate between — got a couple near where I work, and then there's one closer to home that's a bit more relaxed, you know? Cheaper pints, less loud. That's where we tend to end up most weekends.

rows.theme_description: Sometimes someone else flat to cook or chat, as an alternative to the traditional pub option
rows.supporting_quote: But I'd say since covid or whatever, me and my mates have actually started mixing it up a bit more than we used to. Like, we'll do a brewery or go to someone's flat to cook something, watch a film. It's not always the pub anymore

rows.theme_label: Nights at the usual pub have less interaction
rows.theme_description: Getting tired of the same plan to hang out with friends as sometimes you dont even talk
rows.supporting_quote: I think it's just... the pub is so easy to default to that you don't really question it. But you're saying something real there about actually being present. Because you're right, half the time you're checking your phone, someone's got the game on, you're not really talking about anything deep or memorable.

rows.theme_label: Essential to not overthink what to do with your friends
rows.theme_description: Men find it annoying to plan outings too much; they prefer not to make a big deal out of it.
rows.supporting_quote: I suppose we do end up just sitting in the same spot, same as Ibrahim's saying, but I don't think we've got the option to switch it up as much even if we wanted to. And honestly, for us it kind of works because everyone knows where you'll be. You don't need to plan it to death — you just go down there Friday night and your mates are there or they'll be there soon enough.

rows.theme_label: A plant-based diet requires extra effort (eg. time, cooking meals, avilable options, etc.)
rows.theme_description: Changing one's diet is considered a hassle because of the effort it would require and because the environment does not make that transition any easier
rows.supporting_quote:
Right, so here's the thing — this isn't just about whether your mates will judge you. That's one bit of it, yeah, but there's actual practical stuff that gets in the way.

Like, work lunches. I grab something at lunch most days, and options around here are... they're not great if you're actually trying to do plant-based properly. It's not like I'm being picky — there's just not much there. It's either a salad or nothing, and sometimes not even that. So you'd have to start bringing stuff from home, which means planning, which means extra effort. And that's every single day, not just when you're out with mates.

rows.theme_label: Family pressure to keep status quo
rows.theme_description: The family might question these decisions, either because they see them as an attack on the way they cook at home or because they feel other family members are being forced to adopt a new diet or because groceries for the household should change or its disrupting family habits and dynamics
rows.supporting_quote:
Because if I went vegan and it was just about meal planning and bringing stuff to work, that'd be fine. My Thursday lads wouldn't care, I could sort my lunches. But it's the family thing that's different. It's not just Sunday dinner with my mum — it's that if I made that choice, suddenly I'm saying something about how she does things, or what she cares about. And that matters in a way that your mates don't, you know?

And actually, now that I'm thinking about the kids thing — because a couple of my lads are going to be parents — it's even more complicated. Because once you've got a kid, your choices aren't just about you anymore. If you decided to go vegan, you're also deciding that for your kid, at least initially. And that's when people — family, other parents, whoever — they're going to have proper opinions about it. It's not just "oh, he's made a choice," it's "he's forcing his choices on his kid."

rows.theme_label: The pressure to keep status quo will fade eventually, a matter of patience
rows.theme_description: Eventually, the people who initially questioned your decision will get used to your new habits or diet
rows.supporting_quote:
Like, with my Friday group — different from the Thursday lads — one of them started going to the gym seriously, proper diet changes, all of that. And his mum was the same way at first, you know? She'd make comments about him being fussy or whatever. But he just... kept doing it. Didn't make a big thing out of it, didn't argue with her, just quietly got on with his choice. And eventually — and I'm talking months, not weeks — it just became normal. She stopped commenting. It became the thing he does.

So I'm not saying the wear-down isn't real. It is. But I think there's a middle ground between "willpower solves everything" and "it's permanently exhausting." It's maybe just... accepting that there's going to be some awkwardness for a bit, and then it settles down once people realize you're serious and you're not going to be talked out of it.

rows.theme_label: The pubs, its convenient and simpler
rows.theme_description: It is common as it is easy to decide to go there and you can drink, get food, chat and sometimes watch sports
rows.supporting_quote: The pub, really. That's where most of it happens. You can sit down, have a drink, chat without anyone expecting you to be doing anything else. It's low-key. I see the lads maybe once a week or so, and the pub's just the default. It's comfortable, you know? You don't have to plan much — you just meet up, grab a pint, and that's that. Some of us might grab food there too, depending on the pub, but honestly it's more about just being able to sit and talk without the background of life getting in the way.

rows.theme_label: Age leads you to pay more attention to food choices
rows.theme_description: Getting older make you think more of how meals are prepared or where do they come from, not in a strict way more like trying to have better food
rows.supporting_quote:
Thing is, I think I've become more aware of that over the years without really trying to. When you're younger you just eat whatever, don't think about it much. But now, I don't know, you start to actually taste the difference between something that's been looked after and something that's just been... done. And once you've noticed it, you can't unknow it, can you? You go back somewhere and you think, yeah, this is fine, but it's not the same.

I'm not going to pretend I'm checking where everything comes from or anything like that — I still do my shop at Tesco like everyone else. But when you do go to someone who's put the work in, whether that's the local butcher or a pub that's actually bothered, it just... it makes sense. You get what you're paying for. And that matters to me now more than it used to, if I'm being honest.

rows.theme_label: It would be neccesary that plant-based diets would be as common or normal as meat-based diet
rows.theme_description: If it would be as common as a meat-based diet, it would not be questioned so much or at least it would not feel like choosing the less safe choice
rows.supporting_quote:
But right now, I think I'm aware enough of what Amir's saying about it being a safe choice — like, eating meat is the thing you don't have to explain. So it'd have to get to a point where not eating meat was equally... unremarkable? Where nobody would clock it or read something into it. That's the practical bit that's actually about the social stuff, I suppose.

And I mean, I'm not sat here saying I want to go vegetarian anyway, so this is a bit hypothetical. But if I'm being honest about what would need to change, it'd probably be that. The normalcy bit. Because the actual cooking and eating side of it — that's easy enough. It's the other thing that's the blocker.

rows.theme_label: Don't plan meals in advance neither overthinking what to cook
rows.theme_description: It is preferred to be practical at the moment of choosing what to eat, don't give second thoughts to it
rows.supporting_quote: Ah, well, for me, I don't, I don't really think too, too hard about it. It’ll just be, uh, whatever's sort of in the freezer or fridge. I don't plan, plan in detail, uh, in advance or go to the supermarket specifically thinking about what days to buy. I’ll just buy various things, um, I like the look of when I'm in the supermarket and then, as and when decide to eat them. So it's really no specific, um, plan with me, just whatever I fancy on that particular day.

rows.theme_label: Time is a key factor and depends on work schedules, so we don't plan much
rows.theme_description: It depends on the schedule for the week, but we try to be practical—sometimes we order takeout, sometimes we eat out, and sometimes we cook something simple.
rows.supporting_quote:
Yeah, I think it depends what I'm doing. So like, obviously I'm working in, I'm actually on site in the office. I do normally work hybrid. So I usually go in one or two days a week out of the four days that I work. Um, I work in Manchester and live on the whirl. So for me, um, tonight, you know, I've planned for the partner that I will just bung a couple of pizzas in, um, because it's a, you know, it takes 10 minutes. Then obviously we can actually spend a bit of the time in the evening with our kid.
Last night because I was at home working, um, I had actually planned out meals. So I'll, I'll try and have a rough plan based around what the schedule for the week is, but um equally I can get home tonight and go, you know, I can't even be assed cooking a pizza. Let's order a takeaway because, you know, hour long train journey.
So it, it yeah, there's no real plan, um, that we stick to, but I do try to have a bit of a, an idea. But yeah, it's fluid.

rows.theme_label: A practical alternative is to prepare meals that will last for several days and that you know everyone will enjoy
rows.theme_description: It's essential to use your time efficiently, and you don't want to spend too much time preparing meals or learning new recipes
rows.supporting_quote: Yeah, we've got a slow cooker, actually. I was gonna say we've got six people in the house. Um, so, we've kind of got a load of meals that we know everybody, everybody'll eat. And then we tend to batch cook them. I actually work from home most of the time, so I can kind of cook something in the afternoon. But it's really a case of just making these big vats of food that'll last us for a couple of days and just going round with the stuff we know that everyone will eat. So, um, yeah. Yeah, it's not the most adventurous.

rows.theme_label: It's a blessing when your partner cooks—it takes the burden of worrying about meals off your shoulders, and you just eat whatever's there.
rows.theme_description: You don't have to worry about what to eat if you're not the one in charge of preparing meals at home—it's much easier
rows.supporting_quote: Um, well, I'm unemployed at the moment, as is my partner. Um, I'm quite fortunate that she's, um, half Italian and loves to cook. Um, so I kind of don't decide, I'll be honest. Um, so she tends, it's a bit lazy, I must admit, but she tends to, um, make the lunches and dinners and enjoys doing so. I mean, I'll chip in where I can. Um, but as I say, I tend not to decide. Um, we have similar tastes, so that's, that's fine. Um, yeah, but it's, um, it's kind of the decision is taken out of my hands. Um, it wasn't when I was working, but it kind of is at the moment, but I'm, I'm happy to, to go with that at the moment.

rows.theme_label: Price and taste of plant-based are the main barrier
rows.theme_description: Plant-based food should taste very similar to what we're used to and not be too expensive for us to consider making the switch
rows.supporting_quote: For me again, it's down to the price and taste. If it was, if it was cheap and tasted the same, then I'd be perfectly happy to buy it. If it was more expensive, probably less so.

rows.theme_label: Health improvement reason from consuming plant-based
rows.theme_description: If it had health benefits and given that the person engages in physical activity, it would be interesting
rows.supporting_quote: Um, and then if that, yeah, the one that would still really resonate with me is, is just around the, the health, overall fitness. [unintelligible] stock, creaking in my later cricketing years. If I could extend my health, um, further to be able to keep playing for a few more years. So I think something like that would be appealing to me. But I, personally I think, um, protein is a good thing. And meat is a good way of consuming it.

rows.theme_label: Protein is better in meat-based diet
rows.theme_description: It is believed that switching to a plant-based diet would result in an inadequate intake of protein.
rows.supporting_quote: But I, personally I think, um, protein is a good thing. And meat is a good way of consuming it. It's great that it tastes really nice. And I probably know I should eat a little bit less red meat so, sits sits with me. Um, I think it's those health messages.

rows.theme_label: Ingredients in plant-based foods aren't healthier
rows.theme_description: It has been reported that plant-based foods contain fats and sugars that make them unhealthy, so there is considered to be no reason to make them an alternative
rows.supporting_quote: But from what I hear and what I read a lot of these plant based and substitute meals are actually, they're loaded with with with sugars and salts and fats that don't actually make them any healthier for me. So again, maybe if they kind of got a little bit more, uh, adept at producing stuff that that is healthy, a real truthful, um, healthy alternative, then maybe so.
